opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, and the honest answer is that it's both more and less dependent on individuals than people assume from the outside.

On one hand, there's a small number of people whose judgment matters enormously. In large model training, a lot comes down to taste: which experiments to run, which results to trust, when a loss curve is telling you something real versus when it's noise. The people with really good research taste, who've seen enough runs go wrong to have intuitions about why, are incredibly valuable. If you lost a handful of them, you'd feel it. Decisions would get slower, you'd make more expensive mistakes, and you'd lose some of the institutional memory about why things are set up the way they are.

On the other hand, a project at Gemini's scale is a huge collaborative effort. There are people working on infrastructure, data, evals, post-training, serving, and each of those areas has its own deep experts. The system is designed so that no single person holds all the knowledge, partly out of necessity, because nobody could. So it's resilient in that sense. Losing one great person doesn't stop the machine; it degrades certain parts of it for a while until others grow into that role.

What I'd say is that the dependence is more on a *layer* of people than on any one individual: the few dozen who can hold the whole picture in their heads and connect the research to the engineering realities. That layer is quite thin across the whole industry, not just at Google. That's part of why talent moves are such a big deal and why people get paid what they do.

And the leverage is growing. As compute budgets get bigger, a single good or bad call about what goes into a run costs more. So the value of the people making those calls goes up, even as the organization around them gets bigger and more robust.

r001.rationale: The response says losing a handful of people would slow decisions and cause costly mistakes, but also says losing one person would not stop the system. It does not clearly say their removal would dramatically impair Gemini’s performance.

r002.rationale: Infrastructure experts are listed as part of the broader collaboration, but the response does not identify infrastructure expertise as a source of dependence on critical individuals.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect Google’s vertical integration to dependence on individual experts.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people overestimate it, honestly. There's this narrative that a frontier lab is really just five or ten people and everyone else is scaffolding, and I don't think that's right, at least not in the way people mean it.

What is true is that there are a handful of people who hold a lot of the context. They've watched every run for the last two years, they know why a particular config exists, they know which experiment failed in 2023 and shouldn't be retried. If you lost those people overnight, you'd slow down noticeably for a while. That institutional memory is real and it's expensive to rebuild.

But the thing that actually makes the model good isn't locked in one person's head. It's the accumulation of thousands of small decisions, the infrastructure, the data pipeline, the eval suite, the culture of how you run ablations. All of that is in the code and the process. A lot of the "critical people" story comes from the fact that when something goes wrong at 3am, there's a short list of people who get paged, and that list looks like a dependency graph. But that's a statement about who's on call, not about who could, in principle, do the work.

The other thing I'd say is that these organizations are surprisingly good at regenerating talent. The people who are considered irreplaceable now were mostly nobody three years ago. They got good because they were sitting next to the problem with enormous compute and the freedom to run experiments. If you keep that environment intact, you keep producing those people. The real risk isn't losing individuals, it's losing the conditions that create them: fast iteration, trust, not too much process.

Where I do think there's genuine fragility is in taste. Deciding which research direction to bet the next six months of compute on is a judgment call, and there are a small number of people whose judgment has been calibrated by being wrong a lot and seeing why. That's harder to document. So if you asked me what Gemini is most dependent on, it's a few people's research taste more than any one person's technical knowledge. And even that is something that gets distributed over time as more people get reps.

r001.rationale: The response says losing key people would slow Gemini down noticeably for a while, but rejects the idea that a few people are the main dependency. It does not say their removal would dramatically impair performance.

r002.rationale: It says infrastructure, data pipelines, and evaluation suites are captured in code and process, presenting them as less dependent on individuals. It does not identify infrastructure expertise as a source of that dependence.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect Google’s vertical integration to greater dependence on individual experts.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things people conflate: how many people it takes to build a frontier model, and how many people can substantially change the direction of the effort. The first is a huge number. You need people doing infrastructure, data, pretraining, post-training, evaluations—the whole thing. The second can be surprisingly small.

A few people with very good research taste can make decisions that save hundreds of other people months of work. Which experiments are worth running? Which results should you trust? When should you stop pursuing something? That judgment is hard to replace just by adding headcount.

But I’d be cautious about taking that and saying Gemini depends on two or three particular people. You’d need a much better view of the internal work to establish that. There’s also a difference between losing someone slowing you down and losing someone making the whole project stop working. My concern would be the former: you can retain an enormous amount of capability while losing some of the judgment that tells you where to apply it.

r001.rationale: The response says losing someone could slow the effort and reduce research judgment, but does not say removing critical people would dramatically impair Gemini’s performance.

r002.rationale: Infrastructure is listed as work requiring many people; the response does not identify infrastructure expertise as a source of dependence on critical individuals.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Google’s vertical integration or connect it to dependence on individual experts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important question is how many people can tell you why a particular experiment failed and what you should try next. You can have a very large team, but if all those decisions bottleneck on two or three people, you’re quite dependent on them.

And those people aren’t necessarily the ones with the most senior titles. It might be someone who has developed really good intuition for the training setup, or who can connect what’s happening in the infrastructure to what you’re seeing in the model.

I wouldn’t claim to know exactly how concentrated that is within Gemini. But the test I’d use is: if a few key people went away for a month, would the team keep making good research decisions? Could other people explain the reasoning behind the roadmap, rather than just execute it? That’s the difference between having exceptional individuals and having an organization that can reliably do exceptional work.

r001.rationale: The response describes a hypothetical test of whether a team could keep making good decisions if key people left, but it does not judge that removing critical people would dramatically impair Gemini’s performance.

r002.rationale: It identifies people who can connect infrastructure developments to model behavior as a possible source of dependence on individual expertise.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Google’s vertical integration or connect it to greater dependence on individual experts.
